definition: The region of central Italy between the Tiber and the Arno, home to the Etruscan city-states. Its cities, tombs and sanctuaries supply most of the evidence for Etruscan religion.

The people of Etruria and their language, which is usually treated as non-Indo-European. Etruscan texts survive mainly as short inscriptions, and the language was largely replaced by Latin in the Roman period.

A diviner who read the will of the gods in the entrails of sacrificed animals, especially the liver. Roman writers regarded the office as Etruscan, and Roman officials consulted haruspices about prodigies.

The body of Etruscan religious knowledge, covering lightning, entrails, the founding of cities and the interpretation of prodigies. It was preserved in lost books and summarised by Roman writers, who treated it as a distinct tradition.
A bronze model of a sheep's liver, inscribed with the names of gods in Etruscan and found near Piacenza in 1877. It is the best surviving guide to Etruscan hepatoscopy, the reading of livers.
The supreme Etruscan sky god, lord of lightning and counterpart of Roman Jupiter. He forms a triad with Uni and Menerva, and Roman sources attribute three kinds of thunderbolt to him.
The Etruscan queen of the gods, counterpart of Roman Juno. She was honoured as a patron of women, marriage and cities, and her sanctuary at Pyrgi produced inscriptions in Etruscan and Phoenician.
The Etruscan messenger god, counterpart of Greek Hermes and Roman Mercury. He appears on mirrors with winged sandals and serves as a psychopomp, leading the dead toward the underworld.
A winged Etruscan female figure who guides the dead, often shown with a torch, a scroll and a snake. Her name appears in tomb paintings and on sarcophagi, but no myth explains her.
An Etruscan death demon, shown with pointed ears, a heavy brow and a hammer. He guards the underworld in tomb art and is not the same figure as the Greek ferryman Charon.
